slides: That's it, we've reached the last topic in algebra, algebraic understanding. These are algebra questions that don't belong to any one topic we've learned, or that mix a few topics together.

slides.say: Sometimes the solution is algebra, sometimes it's understanding what the givens really say, and sometimes it's one of the tools from psychometric thinking, plugging in numbers or plugging in the answers. To be honest, it's a fairly small part of the exam, and the questions don't repeat themselves. There's no single rule I can give you that solves them all.

But the questions in this topic, and the practice after them, give you tools for questions like these. They help you find a way to solve them. Three tools solve almost all of them. Plug in numbers, plug in the answers, and use the math way and understanding. When the givens allow it, an easy number is often a fast first test. When the numbers don't decide, use the math way.
at: and use the math way and understanding

slides.say: The first tool, plugging in numbers. Say a is any positive number, and the question asks if a squared is always bigger than a. Try a is three. Three squared is nine, and nine is bigger than three. So far, yes.
at: Say a is any positive number

slides.say: But positive numbers can also be between zero and one. Try a is one third. One third squared is one ninth, and one ninth is smaller than one third. So a squared is not always bigger than a. One allowed number where it fails is enough to say not always.

And use only numbers that the givens allow. If the given were different, say a is negative, then three and one third are not allowed. Then we'd try a negative number, like negative two. Negative two squared is four, and four is bigger than negative two.

The second tool, plugging in the answers. Say x squared minus x is six, and the choices are two, three, four and six. We don't have to solve anything. We put each choice into the question. Two squared minus two is four minus two, which is two, not six. Three squared minus three is nine minus three, which is six. So three works.
at: Say x squared minus x is six
the choices are two, three, four and six

slides.say: The third tool, the math way and understanding. Say a plus b is ten, a minus b is four, and they ask for a squared minus b squared. We don't need to find a and b. a squared minus b squared is the bracket a plus b, times the bracket a minus b. That's ten times four, which is forty.
at: Say a plus b is ten
a squared minus b squared is the bracket

slides.say: Understanding also means reading what a given really says. If n is an integer and n is smaller than five, then n is at most four, because there's no integer between four and five. Gaps like this will help us find the biggest or smallest possible value.

slides: As usual, we'll learn the rest through sample questions, where you'll see these tools at work. [pause] I'll see you in the next video.
